feedback: If a child expects the Moon to change within one night, point out the change is slow — compare last night's drawing with tonight's: only a little different.
If a child says the shape is random, lay the drawings in order so the repeat from new → growing → full → shrinking → new becomes visible.
If a child asks why the Moon changes shape, it is fine to say 'we'll find out why when you're a bit older' rather than introducing shadows or a Sun-and-Earth diagram now.
Praise noticing the order and direction of change, not just naming a single shape.
activities.intendedInsight: The Moon's shape changes slowly from night to night over about a month, and the shapes repeat in the same order again and again — it is a predictable pattern, not random.
learnerActions: For about a month, whenever you can see the Moon, draw its shape (at home with a family member helping). The Moon is not up in the evening every night: around new Moon you won't see it at all, and in the 'shrinking' part of the month it rises late, so look for it in the early-morning or daytime sky (never at the Sun). On days you can't see it, write 'not seen'.
Note the date beside each drawing so the record stays in order.
At the end, lay all the drawings out in sequence — a strip or a circle — and look for how the shape changes night to night.
Point to where the Moon grows from a thin sliver to a full round circle, and where it shrinks back down again.
Say out loud what you notice: 'it got thinner', 'tonight it's a full Moon', 'it will grow again'.
activities.title: Month-long Moon diary

feedback: Full understanding: says the sliver will change (not stay the same), uses the recent trend to say which way it is heading, describes the repeating cycle (new → full → back), and justifies it by the pattern — no causal claim needed at this age.
Partial: knows the Moon changes and repeats but can't say which way tonight's sliver is heading or give the order — go back to the ordered diary to make the direction visible.

If a child says a sliver is caused by clouds hiding the rest, point out the dark part isn't grey cloud, it's simply the part we can't see lit; the diary shows the same monthly pattern whatever the weather.

If a child reaches for an Earth's-shadow explanation, stay observational — don't introduce shadow or Sun–Earth–Moon geometry; just secure the repeating pattern and reserve the 'why' for the later orbit topic.
If a child thinks each night is a brand-new different Moon, emphasise it is the same Moon looking different at different times.
activities.intendedInsight: Over two weeks the Moon will definitely change — it will not stay a sliver. Which way it heads (toward full if it has been growing, or toward new if it has been shrinking) is read from the recent trend, and justified by the repeating monthly cycle rather than by the weather.
learnerActions: Consider: tonight the Moon looks like a thin curved sliver. Over the next two weeks, will it stay the same shape or change?
Say what you think it will do — and, importantly, how you know; use what your diary or recent nights have shown about whether the Moon has lately been growing or shrinking.
Talk through what you'd expect after the Moon becomes a full round circle.
activities.title: Predict-and-explain check: will the sliver change?
